title: Hedge Fund Activism, Corporate Governance, and Firm Performance
research_question: Does shareholder activism by hedge funds create value for target firm shareholders, and how does it affect target firms' operating performance, payout policies, capital structure, and executive compensation and turnover? Additionally, which types of firms do activists target, and do any gains to shareholders come at the expense of creditors or managers rather than from genuine value creation?
data_description: The authors construct an original hand-collected dataset of hedge fund activism in U.S. publicly traded firms covering 2001 through 2006. The core sample is built from Schedule 13D filings retrieved via LiveEdgar/EDGAR, supplemented by Schedule 13D/A amendments, Schedule 14A proxy filings, Form 13F holdings from Thomson Financial, and extensive Factiva news searches to capture activism involving stakes below the 5% disclosure threshold. The final sample contains 236 activist hedge funds and 1,059 fund-target pairs covering 882 unique target companies across 183 three-digit SIC industries. Variables include fund stated objectives, tactics, hostility, ownership stakes, holding periods, and outcomes, merged with CRSP daily returns, Compustat accounting data (ROA, EBITDA/Sales, leverage, payout, R&D, Herfindahl indices), I/B/E/S analyst forecasts, ExecuComp executive compensation and CEO turnover data, IRRC governance (G-Index) data, institutional ownership, and Amihud illiquidity measures.
institutional_context: Hedge fund activism emerged in the early 2000s as a distinctive form of shareholder monitoring, contrasting with earlier activism by mutual funds and public pension funds, which faced regulatory diversification requirements, conflicts of interest, political constraints, and weak personal incentives that limited their effectiveness. Hedge funds operate as private partnerships exempt from the Investment Company Act of 1940, can hold concentrated positions, use leverage and derivatives, lock up investor capital, and pay managers performance-based fees (typically 2-and-20). Under Section 13(d) of the 1934 Exchange Act, investors acquiring more than 5% of a public company's shares with intent to influence management must file a Schedule 13D within 10 days, disclosing their purpose under Item 4. This filing serves as a public signal of potential intervention. Activists typically take minority stakes (median around 9.1%) and rely on cooperation from management or support from other shareholders to achieve strategic, operational, financial, or governance changes.
